name: First-wave feminism
summary: First-wave feminism, from Wollstonecraft's 1792 Vindication through the Seneca Falls convention (1848), Mill's Subjection of Women and the suffrage campaigns to about 1920, claimed for women the legal and political standing of men: the vote, the control of their own property and earnings, equal marriage and guardianship law, education and the professions, and one moral standard. It argued from natural rights and the consent of the governed, and from the movement's own texts it said little on economics, foreign policy or most other political questions; strands differed on divorce, religion, the nature of women, and on whether to use militancy.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: Stanton writes in Eighty Years and More (England, 1887): "I detest the words 'royalty' and 'nobility,' and all the ideas and institutions based on their recognition." Wollstonecraft likewise blames hereditary honours, titles and hereditary power for idleness and mischief and hopes nobles will throw off their "hereditary trappings."

arbitrator-settles-disputes.rationale: The editors (Stanton, Anthony, Gage) write in the HWS vol. 1 Introduction that the Geneva Arbitration of the Alabama Claims between England and America "pointed the way for the future adjustment of all national difficulties".

character-from-environment.rationale: Wollstonecraft argues character is formed by education and circumstance, comparing women's education-induced weakness to that of soldiers sent into the world unprepared and of courtiers whose character despotism had formed (Vindication, chs. 2 and 4).

distinct-gender-roles.rationale: The Declaration of Sentiments condemns man for claiming "as his right to assign for her a sphere of action" and insists women have "immediate admission to all the rights and privileges which belong to them as citizens", so it rejects laws assigning different public roles by sex.

duties-before-rights.rationale: In Solitude of Self, Stanton puts first what belongs to woman "as an individual" and says her rights and duties are "individual happiness and development", with only "incidental relations of life" such as wife and mother involving special duties.

dynastic-succession.rationale: Wollstonecraft's Vindication (Introduction) speaks of the 'wretchedness that has flowed from hereditary honours, riches, and monarchy', and later says 'hereditary power chokes the affections', condemning inherited rule.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: The Declaration says 'all men and women are created equal' and the 1860s Equal Rights Association resolutions demanded rights for women and colored people alike, but in 1869 Stanton and others opposed manhood suffrage with arguments ranking educated women above black men, and the movement split over the Fifteenth Amendment; the record is mixed.

filial-duty.rationale: Wollstonecraft, ch. 11 (Duty to Parents), holds that a parent who attended to a child's helpless infancy "has a right to require the same attention when the feebleness of age comes upon him"; she makes this reciprocal duty conditional on the parent having done that care.

free-trade.rationale: Stanton's 1866 open letter as an independent candidate for Congress (HWS vol. 2) gives her creed as "free speech, free press, free men, and free trade" and faults protection as "the narrowest selfishness in trade between nations"; in her 1867 address she also cites "the wisdom, the beneficence, the morality of free trade".

gender-social-construct.rationale: Wollstonecraft argues women's weakness and artificial character are produced by education and circumstance ("made by her education the slave of sensibility"), and LibreTexts reports first-wave feminists held women were only "inferior" because of their inferior education.

god-not-male.rationale: In her signed comment on the Gospels in Woman's Bible Part II (1898), Stanton asks 'If a Heavenly Father was necessary, why not a Heavenly Mother?', objecting to a purely male picture of the divine.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: In the Woman's Bible, Stanton (commentary on Kings) condemns Bible-derived rules about women that have been "incorporated into the laws of both England and the United States" as a union of Church and State, and says canon law framed by the priesthood made women subordinate in civil law.

military-force-beyond-defence.rationale: Wollstonecraft (Vindication, ch. 9) calls "defensive war, the only justifiable war, in the present advanced state of society", and hopes to see the bayonet converted into a pruning hook.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: Stanton (Eighty Years and More, 1887) detests "royalty" and "all the ideas and institutions based on" it, and Wollstonecraft attacks "the sacred majesty of kings" and the wretchedness flowing from hereditary honours and monarchy; neither carves out a ceremonial monarch.

no-duty-to-obey.rationale: Stanton and Anthony's own 1868 Revolution creed (reprinted in HWS vol. 2) holds individual rights are "above all constitutions, customs, creeds, and codes" and resistance to tyranny a duty; Eighty Years and More says it looked "as imperative a duty" as aiding a fugitive slave to defy an unjust law by helping a woman escape recapture from an asylum.

no-fault-divorce.rationale: Stanton and Blackwell argued at the 1860 national convention that divorce reform belonged on the platform, while Wendell Phillips objected to the resolutions as outside a woman's-rights convention, and an 1872 convention resolved that suffrage means 'greater permanency in marriage'; the movement took no common line.

patriarchy-structural.rationale: The Declaration of Sentiments charges that "the history of mankind is a history of repeated injuries and usurpations on the part of man toward woman, having in direct object the establishment of an absolute tyranny over her", then lists the laws and customs (franchise, property, marriage, employment, education) that favour men.

property-franchise.rationale: The Address to Congress adopted by the Eleventh National Woman's Rights Convention in 1866 (HWS vol. 2, ch. 18) declares that 'All prohibitions based on race, color, sex, property, or education, are violations of the republican idea', and its resolution that year demanded universal suffrage.

punish-blasphemy.rationale: In Eighty Years and More (ch. XXII, her 1880s English visit) Stanton says the blasphemy trials of Foote and Ramsey 'seemed unworthy a great nation in the nineteenth century' and that 'Whatever is true can stand investigation and ridicule', so she opposes prosecuting blasphemy.

racial-franchise.rationale: The 1866 Eleventh National Woman's Rights Convention Address to Congress (HWS vol. 2, ch. 18) asks that the principles of government be secured 'to ALL ... without distinction of race, color or sex', and the convention resolved to demand 'UNIVERSAL SUFFRAGE' under the American Equal Rights Association.

racial-oppression-before-sexism.rationale: In her 1865 letter "This is the Negro's hour" (HWS vol. 2) Stanton refuses to stand aside while Black men are enfranchised first and demands rights for women and men together; she and Anthony then founded the NWSA in protest at the Fifteenth Amendment leaving women out.

religion-oppresses-women.rationale: Stanton wrote that she found no explanation for the degraded status of women 'under all religions' and published the Woman's Bible, while suffrage and temperance conventions passed resolutions against it and Willard declined to take part; adherents split.

religious-offensive-war.rationale: Wollstonecraft (Vindication, ch. 9) holds defensive war to be "the only justifiable war" in advanced society, so a war begun to bring peoples under a religion is not justified; the HWS vol. 1 Introduction likewise calls war a feature of barbarism.

sacred-ruler.rationale: Wollstonecraft opens by "attacking the sacred majesty of kings" and calls the reverence paid to kings "an insult to reason"; the HWS vol. 1 introduction (ch. 1) welcomes the replacement of the divine right of kings by individual conscience and judgment.

scripture-inerrant.rationale: Stanton's preface to Woman's Bible Part II (1898) says the Bible's degrading ideas of woman 'emanated from the brain of man' rather than God, and 'We have made a fetich of the Bible long enough'. Her own suffrage association disowned the book, so this is her stated position rather than the whole movement's, hence -1 not -2.

scripture-judged-by-women.rationale: Stanton's Woman's Bible examined what the scriptures say of women and held the texts to no special authority, but suffrage and temperance conventions disapproved of it by resolution and Willard and others withdrew from the revising committee; strands split.

self-ownership.rationale: The 1850s resolutions condemn marriage law that denies a wife 'the product of her own industry' and 'the custody of her own person', and Stanton grounds women's claims on a 'birthright to self-sovereignty'; the sources do not use the libertarian term.

shared-human-nature.rationale: A Seneca Falls resolution (HWS vol. 1, ch. 4) states that "the equality of human rights results necessarily from the fact of the identity of the race in capabilities and responsibilities", grounding women's rights in a common human nature.

shared-marital-authority.rationale: The Declaration of Sentiments condemns the marriage covenant in which the wife must promise obedience and the husband becomes her "master", and the law's "supremacy of man"; it demands equal standing for the wife in marriage.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: The Declaration of Sentiments (1848) says a long train of abuses designed to establish "absolute despotism" makes it the duty of the people to throw off such government, and Wollstonecraft condemns "lawless power" and "arbitrary power" and rejects the divine right of kings.

universal-morality.rationale: Wollstonecraft argues that virtue has "only one eternal standard" and that truth is "a simple principle, which admits of no modification", so the same moral principles bind both sexes (Vindication, ch. 2).

war-builds-character.rationale: Wollstonecraft (Vindication, ch. 9) says the present system of war has "little connection with virtue" and is "rather the school of finesse and effeminacy, than of fortitude"; the HWS vol. 1 Introduction calls war "merely a feature of barbarism".

wife-divorce-without-consent.rationale: Stanton records in Eighty Years that she demanded a statute allowing wives an absolute divorce for their husbands' brutality and intemperance, and she spoke to the New York legislature for a liberal divorce law in 1860 (HWS vol. 1); the Sentiments also condemn divorce laws giving all power to the husband.

women-in-religious-leadership.rationale: The Sentiments protest women's exclusion from the ministry, the Seneca Falls resolutions claim women's right to teach in all religious assemblies, and Stanton says she steadily demanded that women be ordained and hold the offices of elder, deacon and trustee (Eighty Years).

women-property-inheritance.rationale: The Declaration of Sentiments charges that man "has taken from her all right in property, even to the wages she earns", and HWS vol. 1 celebrates the New York laws of 1848-1860 giving married women their own inheritance to use, will and dispose of.

women-suffrage.rationale: Seneca Falls Declaration of Sentiments (1848) charges that man 'has never permitted her to exercise her inalienable right to the elective franchise' and insists women have 'immediate admission to all the rights and privileges which belong to them as citizens'; the vote was the movement's central demand (HWS vol. 2, ch. 18, 1866 Address to Congress: ballot 'in the hand of every man and woman').

missingStatements.text: Women should receive equal pay for equal work.
missingStatements.rationale: The 1851 Indiana convention resolved that 'woman should receive for equal labor, equal pay with man' and later conventions demanded equal pay for equal work.
missingStatements.declined: Accepted almost everywhere today, so not contested.

missingStatements.text: Men and women should be held to the same standard of sexual conduct.
missingStatements.rationale: A Seneca Falls resolution says the same virtue and delicacy required of woman should be required of man and the same transgressions visited with equal severity on both; the Declaration condemns a 'different code of morals for men and women'.

keyFigures.role: Principal author of the 1848 Declaration of Sentiments and a founder of the National Woman Suffrage Association

evidence.quote: First-wave feminism refers to a significant social and political movement that occurred primarily during the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, focusing primarily on women's rights, especially the right to vote. Influenced by early feminist thinkers like Mary Wollstonecraft, the movement was spearheaded by figures such as Elizabeth Cady Stanton and Lucretia Mott.

First-wave feminism occurred throughout the world in the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries and mainly focused on fighting for women's right to vote. The wave was influenced by Mary Wollstonecraft and begun by Elizabeth Cady Stanton and Lucretia Mott.

White middle-class first wave feminists in the 19th century to early 20th century, such as suffragist leaders Elizabeth Cady Stanton and Susan B. Anthony, primarily focused on women’s suffrage (the right to vote), striking down coverture laws, and gaining access to education and employment.

Elizabeth Cady Stanton, Lucretia Mott, and Susan B. Anthony all worked together as women’s rights advocates. They were considered some of the most influential first-wave feminists through their efforts in the suffrage movement.

scope: First-wave feminism as the sources describe it: the organised movement of the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, chiefly in the United States and Britain, from the 1848 Seneca Falls Convention to the 19th Amendment (1920) and Britain's Equal Franchise Act (1928), for women's legal and political equality: above all the vote, but also property, marriage, divorce, education and employment (EBSCO Research Starters; the UMass Amherst open textbook; Simply Psychology; LibreTexts; TheCollector). The texts it ties to the movement are the 1848 Declaration of Sentiments, Wollstonecraft's Vindication of the Rights of Woman (1792) and the writings of its leading figure Elizabeth Cady Stanton (the History of Woman Suffrage, Eighty Years and More, the Woman's Bible, her letters and diary, and her 1892 address 'Solitude of Self'). It excludes second- and third-wave feminism, and the platforms of particular organisations (NWSA, AWSA, WSPU, WCTU) beyond what these sources report of the movement; the militant British suffragettes and the exclusion of Black and working-class women enter only as the defining sources report them.

evidence.quote: First-wave feminists were often involved in other reform movements, including temperance and abolition, which helped shape their activism. A landmark event in this wave was the Seneca Falls Convention, where the Declaration of Sentiments was drafted, outlining grievances and demands for women's equality.

White middle-class first wave feminists in the 19th century to early 20th century, such as suffragist leaders Elizabeth Cady Stanton and Susan B. Anthony, primarily focused on women’s suffrage (the right to vote), striking down coverture laws, and gaining access to education and employment. These goals are famously enshrined in the Seneca Falls Declaration of Sentiments, which is the resulting document of the first women’s rights convention in the United States in 1848.

Definition: First-wave feminism was the first organised women’s movement, running roughly from the 1848 Seneca Falls Convention to 1928, centred on winning suffrage alongside property, education and legal-identity rights. Seneca Falls: The 1848 Seneca Falls Convention and its Declaration of Sentiments launched the US campaign and made the vote its central, unifying goal.

The first wave of feminism officially began with the first women’s rights meeting at the Seneca Falls Convention in 1848. The initial idea for the convention came in 1840 at the World Anti-Slavery Convention in London. Women weren’t invited to attend the event. Despite being a men-only event, some women activists, including Elizabeth Cady Stanton and Lucretia Mott, still decided to show. Their unwelcomed attendance led to the men excluding them from speaking or participating in any discussions, but they were allowed to stay. Stanton and Mott met on July 9, 1848, at the home of philanthropists Jane and Richard Hunt in Waterloo, New York to organize the first women’s rights convention. evidence.quote: The history of first-wave feminism 18th Century: Intellectual Foundations Before the movement formally organized, individual thinkers challenged the patriarchal status quo , arguing that women possessed the same rational capacity for citizenship as men . 1792 : Mary Wollstonecraft publishes A Vindication of the Rights of Woman .

First-wave feminism occurred throughout the world in the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries and mainly focused on fighting for women's right to vote. The wave was influenced by Mary Wollstonecraft and begun by Elizabeth Cady Stanton and Lucretia Mott. First-wave feminism was heavily intertwined with both the temperance and abolitionist movements. First-wave feminists accomplished their primary goal in 1920 when the US government amended its Constitution to give all women the right to vote, but many of their secondary goals remained unaccomplished. Second- and third-wave feminists focused on these goals, rallying against conservative gender roles, unequal pay, and other forms of discrimination. Background Feminism refers to a political or social movement that pushes for equality for women. Before the first feminists, women had few legal rights. In most parts of the world, they were not allowed to own property, vote, or hold political office. Mary Wollstonecraft, a well-known early feminist, independently earned her living through writing and translating. She published several notable feminist pieces, including Thoughts on the Education of Daughters (1787), Maria, or the Wrongs of Woman (1798), and A Vindication of the Rights of Woman (1792).
